What lives outside the BMF

Source: vignettes/outside-the-bmf.Rmd
outside-the-bmf.Rmd

An automated cascade either finds a grant recipient in the IRS Business Master File or it does not. Adjudicating the MAYBE tier is about the cases where it found several candidates and could not choose. This one is about the cases where it found nothing worth offering — and the first thing to say is that most of them are not matching failures at all.

Of 91 randomly drawn NO identities, 53 are payees the Business Master File could never contain. Individuals collecting scholarships, businesses, government bodies, foreign organisations, and placeholders like SEE SCHEDULE ATTACHED. Only 33 are organisations the file should list and the cascade missed. The honest floor — real bodies with no exemption of their own — is 6.

The tier this is about

status identities share of 4,903 meaning
YES 2979 60.76% accepted automatically
MAYBE 1044 21.29% candidates surfaced, none decisive
NO 845 17.23% nothing surfaced, or all of it vetoed
OOS 35 0.71% flagged out of sample before matching

845, not 725

The published baseline reports 725 NO. pf_status() reports 845, and the gap is the interesting part.

shape identities in the baseline’s denominator
retrieved something, scored below the floor 725 yes
no blocking pass produced any pair at all 120 no

pf_status() runs over every identity in the file. The tiered result runs only over identities that got at least one scored candidate. 120 in-scope identities never reached the result frame because no blocking pass produced any pair at all — and so the baseline’s denominator of 4,748 excludes the cases retrieval failed on hardest.

denominator n what YES alone
result frame 4748 identities with at least one scored candidate 62.74%
in scope 4868 every identity the cascade should have resolved 61.20%
whole file 4903 every identity in the population file 60.76%

On the in-scope denominator the same run is 61.20%, not 62.74%. That is not a defect in the arm; it is a statement about which figure answers which question. A match rate cannot drop the grants its retrieval step never reached. Everything below is reported against 4,868.

Why there is one arm and no cost frontier

The MAYBE experiment compared a cheap model, an expensive one, and the expensive one with web search, because all three could answer its question: the correct EIN was already in the candidate set 71% of the time, so a reviewer confined to the packet had something real to decide.

Here it is not. A NO case has no candidate worth offering, so when there is an answer it is outside the packet 100% of the time. A model without search can only report that the filed name does not resemble the records already rejected, which is what the cascade said. So there is one arm, it has search, and no cheaper strategy is benchmarked because none applies.

That asymmetry is itself a finding: the MAYBE tier supports a cost/quality frontier and the NO tier does not.

What a reviewer is given

The filed record — name, street, city, state, ZIP, stated purpose, amount, tax year, and the foundation’s own recipient-status text, all uncontrolled filer free text. The filing foundation, as context. And then one of two things:

  • no candidate retrieved (12 of the 100 cases): nothing to show, the reviewer works from the filed record alone
  • the rejected near-misses, with their scores (88 cases): the records the cascade found and declined

The near-misses are shown deliberately. In the prior hand audit the correct record had already been offered in most recoverable cases, so hiding them would hide the dominant mechanism.

They are also a trap, and the schema is built around it. An EIN read off a near-miss row is in the reference by construction — it got there because the blocker pulled it out of the reference — so counting it as evidence that the reference covers this tier is circular. Every verdict therefore records whether its EIN came from the web or from a candidate row, and the headline uses web-sourced EINs only.

As it happened, all 34 EINs in the estimation stratum were web-sourced and none was read off a candidate row, so the guard had nothing to exclude. That was not guaranteed; it is why it was built.

How much of the tier is recoverable

n share 95% Wilson
an EIN was established at all 34 of 91 37.4%
and that EIN is in the reference 33 of 91 36.3% [27.1%, 46.5%]

That projects to ~306 of the 845 NO identities, [229, 393].

“Recoverable” here means: the investigation established an EIN from an outside source, and that EIN is in the reference. It is a mechanical set-membership test — the model never saw the reference and was told so. It is not a verified match: an EIN can be in the reference and still belong to the wrong organisation. The head-to-head below is the only check on that.

Is the right EIN already in the reference?

This is the question that decides whether the NO tier is a coverage problem or a name problem.

in the reference
estimation stratum 33 of 34 — 97.1%
both strata 37 of 38 — 97.4% [86.5%, 99.5%]

The single exception is COMMONWEALTH UNIV OF PENN, EIN 23-2738930, which the model classed GOVERNMENT — a Pennsylvania state university. A governmental unit is not an exempt organisation, so the file is correct to omit it.

Zero genuine coverage gaps in 38 independently established EINs. The earlier audit found 21 of 21 on a narrower population; this confirms it on the production tier at nearly double the n. Widening the reference will not shrink this residual, because the reference already contains it.

Why the cascade missed them

For the 37 recoverable cases, was the correct EIN ever put in front of the scorer? Every scored pair is cached, so this is a lookup rather than a replay of the blocker.

cause diagnosis n share
offered to the scorer and rejected a scoring / threshold failure 26 70.3%
never offered at all a blocking / retrieval failure 11 29.7%

Where it was offered, the score the comparator gave the correct row was a median of 0.360, ranging 0.080 to 0.622, against a review floor of 0.65. Only 2 of 26 reached even 0.60.

So the dominant failure is not retrieval. In 70% of recoverable cases the right record was in hand and ranked far below the floor.

hypothesis never offered offered
LEGAL_NAME_DIFFERS 2 7
TRUNCATED 1 6
DBA_OR_TRADE_NAME 3 4
PARENT_OR_CHAPTER 0 5
ACRONYM 1 1
GEOGRAPHY_WRONG 1 1
PROGRAM_NAMED 1 1
PLAIN_MISS 0 1
TYPO 2 0

Two patterns are worth naming.

TYPO is never retrieved. THE WESMINSTER SCHOOL and COCORDIA UNIVERSITY each scored no candidates at all. A misspelling inside the one distinctive token destroys the only key an inverted name-token index could have used. No comparator can rescue a case that never reaches it.

PARENT_OR_CHAPTER is always retrieved and always underscored. Four of the five are SALVATION ARMY and YOUNG LIFE at 0.08 — a name that cannot discriminate between hundreds of real records, where the geography term correctly refuses to break the tie. These should not be forced through: loosening there buys wrong EINs.

The two call for opposite fixes, which is why reporting them as one “name resolution” number would be useless.

What lives outside the BMF, and why

entity_class n share ~of 845
INDIVIDUAL 39 42.9% 362
NONPROFIT 27 29.7% 251
FOREIGN 5 5.5% 46
GOVERNMENT 5 5.5% 46
GROUP_SUBORDINATE 5 5.5% 46
AGGREGATE 3 3.3% 28
CHURCH 3 3.3% 28
PROGRAM_OR_EVENT 2 2.2% 19
FISCALLY_SPONSORED 1 1.1% 9
FOR_PROFIT 1 1.1% 9

Rolled up by whether a record should exist at all:

n share 95% Wilson
not an organisation the BMF could ever hold 53 of 91 58.2% [48.0%, 67.8%]
a real body the BMF should list 33 of 91 36.3% [27.1%, 46.5%]
a real body with no exemption of its own 6 of 91 6.6% [3.1%, 13.6%]
could not be identified at all 0 of 91 0.0%

Not an organisation (58.2%)

The largest group in the tier by a wide margin. 39 individuals — almost all scholarship payments to named students — plus 5 government bodies (a high school, a public elementary school, a county fire and rescue department, a state university, a university research institute), 5 foreign organisations (a Polish foundation, UNIDROIT, a UK charity, a BC society, the ICRC), 3 aggregate placeholders, and 1 for-profit.

These reached the matching path, where they can only fail or match something wrong. They are a denominator problem, not a matching problem.

And the pipeline’s own signals largely did not catch them:

signal catches recall false positives
looks_personal is TRUE 11 of 39 28.2% 0 of 11
filed status code reads individual 19 of 39 48.7% not measured here

Every case looks_personal flagged really is an individual — 11 of 11, no false positives — and it misses 28 of 39. A precise, low-recall flag is the easy kind to fix: nothing needs to become more conservative, the 202-name given-name list simply has to get longer. Seven payees that are not organisations at all are affirmatively coded public_charity by the filed status field, which is why that field cannot be trusted on its own.

A real body with no exemption of its own (6.6%)

The honest floor. Two churches (SEVIER HEIGHTS BAPTIST CHURCH, ST AGNES CHURCH), which are exempt without applying and need not file; a diocesan high school under a group ruling; one fiscally sponsored project; and two named events. There is no EIN to find, so no amount of matching recovers these.

At 6.6% this is much smaller than the prior audit’s 12-in-100 estimate for the same category. The floor is a few percent, not a tenth.

Could not be identified at all (0%)

Search identified something in every one of the 91 cases. The prior audit, which searched 46 of its 67 adjudicated cases, had 10 “no such organisation traceable”. With search applied to every case that category disappears.

Why entity_class and bmf_expectation are separate fields

The INTERNATIONAL COMMITTE OF THE RED CROSS case earns the distinction. The model classed it FOREIGN, which is right — it is Swiss — and bmf_expectation LISTED, which is also right, because it holds a US exemption record. The EIN it reported is in the reference.

Collapsing “what the entity is” into “should a record exist” would have scored that case wrong whichever way it collapsed. A Scout troop is a subordinate and is not listed; a Salvation Army area command is a subordinate and is. They are different questions.

Does a human agree?

Almost everything above is the model’s judgement, so it needs a check against something other than the model’s own confidence.

An earlier hand audit adjudicated 67 NO cases. Re-keyed on the filed recipient name, 63 of them are still NO identities in this arm, so the same arm was run over exactly those 63 and the two sides compared. Both judged the same organisations from the same filed record; the only difference is who judged.

human’s class model agreed
not an organisation 11 of 11 100.0%
a real body the BMF should list 30 of 34 88.2%
no exemption of its own 5 of 6 83.3%
could not be identified 3 of 8 37.5%

Overall 49 of 59 — 83.1% [71.5%, 90.5%], Cohen’s kappa 0.724. Four cases the human marked unclear are excluded; a non-answer cannot agree or disagree with anything.

Three of the ten disagreements exist only because this comparison maps the human’s “geography unclear” verdict to recoverable. All three are churches. Dropping that hedge gives 87.5% and kappa 0.795 — the figure above keeps the conservative reading.

The one class they diverge on is the reassuring part

37.5% on “could not be identified” looks alarming until the cases are read. Of the 8 the human could not trace, the model agreed on exactly 3 — and those 3 are precisely the ones where it reported low confidence and named no organisation.

On the other 5 it found something at medium or high confidence. DOCKS TO DOORWAYS is a Belgrade Lakes Association campaign, and the filed street field literally reads PO Box 551 Belgrade Lakes Associati[on]. AMERICAN SHRINE ASSOCIATES sits at the Basilica of the National Shrine’s address. 505 Main Street Canton is not a name at all, it is a street address, and the depot there is run by a food pantry.

The model’s confidence tracks the disagreement exactly: where it says low it agrees the case is untraceable, and where it says medium or high it found what the human could not. That is the opposite of the pattern the MAYBE search arm showed, where confidence rose while accuracy fell. Here confidence is worth routing on.

On the EIN itself, which needs no vocabulary mapping

Both sides name an EIN on 24 cases and give the same nine digits on 23 — 95.8%. The exception is The Salvation Army: the model gives the Illinois corporation, the human the Southern territory. Both EINs are real; which is correct depends on which corporation received the money.

The model named an EIN on 11 cases where the human could not, and all 11 are in the reference — 5 of them cases the human had already called a real organisation without being able to produce its number.

The human named one where the model declined: Hamilton Co Gen Hlt Dist. It is a county health district, the model called it government, and that EIN is the one human EIN not in the reference. The model was right to refuse it.

Both sides land in the same place

recoverable, of the same 63
human 34 — 54.0%
model 35 — 55.6%
independently established EINs in the reference
model 33 of 33 — 100%
human 24 of 25 — 96.0%

Neither side found a single genuine coverage gap.

Where that leaves the match rate

numerator on 4,868 in scope
YES alone 61.20%
YES + recovered NO 67.49%
YES + cleared MAYBE 77.11%
YES + cleared MAYBE + recovered NO 83.40%

Recovering the NO tier is worth +6.29 points. But dropping the payees that are not organisations the file could ever hold — ~492 identities, taking the denominator from 4,868 to 4,376 — moves YES alone from 61.20% to 68.08%, a gain of +6.88 points, while matching precisely nothing.

The scope correction is worth more than the recovery. Only one of the two is a matching improvement; the other is a statement about which grants were ever answerable. Both should be reported, and neither should be quietly folded into a headline.

What this does not establish

  • Recoverability is not accuracy. 36.3% of the tier has an EIN that exists in the reference. Whether it is the correct EIN rests on the head-to-head above and on the model’s own confidence, not on the set-membership test.
  • The taxonomy is a model’s judgement. The mechanical parts — is the EIN in the reference, was it ever offered, what did it score — are not. The split between them is deliberate and the two should not be quoted with equal confidence.
  • One adjudicator on each side. The human labels come from a single pass with no blind second review, and the model ran once at one effort level. Neither is a consensus.
  • UNCERTAIN was barely used. One case of 100. A reviewer that almost never declines is either very well calibrated or is resolving ambiguity it should be surfacing; 100 cases cannot separate those.
  • The 120 never-scored identities are 12 cases in this sample. Their composition is reported with everything else, but a 12-case subset supports no claim of its own.
  • Search cost is not in the token figure. $0.0669 per case in tokens, plus 3.2 web searches per case billed separately. No ratio to the MAYBE arms is quoted: those were computed on that experiment’s own runs, some logged before the cache-write accounting was corrected.

Reproducing 

PFMATCH_DIR=. Rscript dev/adjudicate-10-no-packet.R    # re-runs the match, ~30 min
Rscript dev/adjudicate-11-no-search.R
Rscript dev/adjudicate-12-no-score.R

PF_NO_SET=cal Rscript dev/adjudicate-10-no-packet.R    # the human head-to-head
PF_NO_SET=cal Rscript dev/adjudicate-11-no-search.R
Rscript dev/adjudicate-14-no-calib.R

The packet stage gates every identity’s tier against BASELINE-2026-10C and stops on any drift, because a sample drawn from a drifted run does not describe the baseline’s NO tier and its recovery could not be added to the baseline’s match rate. It also re-checks that it drew the same 100 ids as the cached packet, so a rebuild cannot silently leave collected verdicts keyed to different case text.

Design, full read-out and the taxonomy definitions are in dev/NO-TIER-EXPERIMENT.md; the reviewer’s instructions are dev/LLM-NO-INSTRUCTIONS.md.
